subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 14! In this unit you will learn how to describe exactly where a shape sits and exactly how it moves. These are two of the most useful ideas in all of geometry. Every time Amina gives directions to her house in Hargeisa, every time Yusuf reads a map of the route to the masjid, and every time a game designer moves a character across the screen, they are using position and transformation.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics 0862 — Stage 7 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Plot and read points in all four quadrants using coordinate pairs (x, y), including negative values.
Name the origin, the x-axis, the y-axis and the four quadrants, and know the sign pattern of each quadrant.
Describe and perform a translation using a column vector and describe it in words.
Describe and perform a reflection in a mirror line, including the x-axis, the y-axis and lines such as x = 2.
Describe and perform a rotation about a point, giving the centre, angle and direction.
Use coordinate rules to transform points quickly with algebra.
Explain why translations, reflections and rotations produce a congruent image, and combine two transformations in sequence.
Find the distance between two coordinate points that share the same x-coordinate or the same y-coordinate, without needing to draw a grid.
Enlarge a shape by a positive integer scale factor from a centre of enlargement, and explain why the image is similar (but not congruent) to the object.

concepts.title: The Coordinate Grid and Four Quadrants
concepts.explanation: A coordinate grid (also called the coordinate plane) is built from two number lines that cross at right angles. The horizontal line is the x-axis and the vertical line is the y-axis. They meet at a single point called the origin, whose coordinates are (0, 0). Every other point on the grid has its own unique pair of numbers, just as every house on a well-planned street has its own address. Positive and negative signs tell you the direction. A positive x means move right; a negative x means move left. A positive y means move up; a negative y means move down.
concepts.example: The two axes cut the grid into four regions called quadrants, numbered with Roman numerals and running anticlockwise from the top-right:

concepts.title: Plotting and Reading Points Accurately
concepts.explanation:
Plotting means marking a point when you are given its coordinates. Reading means writing the coordinates of a point you can already see. These are opposite skills, and you need both. To plot a point, start at the origin every single time. Move along the x-axis by the first number, then move parallel to the y-axis by the second number, and make a small neat cross where you land.

To read a point, do the reverse. Look at the point and ask two questions. First, how far left or right of the y-axis is it? That distance, with the correct sign, is the x-coordinate. Second, how far above or below the x-axis is it? That distance, with the correct sign, is the y-coordinate. Always check the signs carefully: a point to the left of the y-axis has a negative x, and a point below the x-axis has a negative y.

Here is a common trap to avoid. Many learners rush and swap the two numbers, plotting (2, 5) where (5, 2) belongs. Slow down and whisper the rule – x first, then y; along, then up. Another trap is to lose track of the sign when working in the lower or left quadrants. If Khadija plots the vertices of a triangle and one corner drifts into the wrong quadrant, the whole triangle will look wrong. Careful, unhurried plotting is the foundation of every transformation that follows in this unit.
concepts.example: Coordinates also let us describe whole shapes. A rectangle might have corners, called vertices, at (1, 1), (5, 1), (5, 3) and (1, 3). If you plot those four points and join them in order with a ruler, a rectangle appears. Because we can describe a shape entirely by its vertices, we can move the whole shape simply by moving each vertex – and that is exactly how the transformations in this unit work. Master plotting now, and every later idea becomes much easier.

concepts.title: Translation – Sliding a Shape
concepts.explanation:
A translation slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction. Nothing turns and nothing flips – the shape just moves to a new position, keeping exactly the same size, shape and orientation. Sliding a book across a table, moving a game piece across a board, or shifting a chair straight across a room are all everyday translations.

We describe a translation with a column vector, two numbers written one above the other. The top number tells you the horizontal move (right is positive, left is negative). The bottom number tells you the vertical move (up is positive, down is negative). For example, the vector (3 over -2) means ‘move 3 units right and 2 units down’. Because writing a column in a line of text is awkward, we will write it here as (3, -2) with the understanding that the first number is horizontal and the second is vertical.

To translate a shape, apply the same slide to every vertex. Suppose a triangle has vertices at A(1, 1), B(4, 1) and C(1, 3), and we translate it by (3, -2). We add 3 to each x-coordinate and subtract 2 from each y-coordinate. So A(1, 1) moves to A′(4, -1), B(4, 1) moves to B′(7, -1), and C(1, 3) moves to C′(4, 1). Plot the new points, join them, and you have an identical triangle that has simply slid across the grid. We call the original the object and the new one the image, and we mark image points with a small dash, like A′, read aloud as ‘A dash’ or ‘A prime’.
concepts.example: Two useful facts make translations powerful. First, the image is always congruent to the object – same size, same shape, same way up. Second, if you do one translation and then another, the results add together. Sliding by (3, -2) and then by (1, 4) gives the same finish as a single slide of (4, 2), because 3 + 1 = 4 and -2 + 4 = 2. This is why complex movements in animation and robotics can be built from simple slides added together. To undo a translation, reverse both numbers: the inverse of (3, -2) is (-3, 2).

concepts.title: Reflection – Flipping in a Mirror Line
concepts.explanation:
A reflection produces a mirror image of a shape across a straight line called the mirror line or line of reflection. When you look in a mirror you see yourself the same size and shape but reversed left to right; mathematical reflection works in exactly the same way. The reflected image is congruent to the object, but its orientation is flipped.

The mirror line follows one golden rule: every point of the image is the same distance from the mirror line as the matching point of the object, but on the opposite side. The line joining a point to its image crosses the mirror line at a right angle. So if a corner sits 3 units to the left of the mirror line, its image sits 3 units to the right of that same line, directly across from it.

To reflect a shape neatly, reflect each vertex and then join the images. Measure the perpendicular distance from each vertex to the mirror line, then count the same distance across to the other side and mark the image point. A piece of tracing paper is a wonderful check: trace the shape and the mirror line, flip the paper over along the line, and the tracing should land exactly on the image you drew.

Reflections in the axes have especially tidy coordinate rules, which you will use again and again:

Reflection in the x-axis: the rule is (x, y) → (x, -y). The x stays the same; the y changes sign. So (3, 2) becomes (3, -2).

Reflection in the y-axis: the rule is (x, y) → (-x, y). The y stays the same; the x changes sign. So (3, 2) becomes (-3, 2).

Reflection in a vertical line like x = 2: measure how far the point is from the line and count the same distance across. (5, 1) is 3 right of x = 2, so its image is 3 left, at (-1, 1).
concepts.example: Reflection is closely tied to symmetry. A shape has a line of symmetry when reflecting it in that line leaves it looking exactly the same – you could fold the shape along the line and the two halves would match perfectly. A square has four lines of symmetry, an equilateral triangle has three, and a circle has infinitely many, since any line through its centre is a line of symmetry. You can see this beautiful balance in the geometric patterns of tilework and woven mats, and in the wings of a butterfly.

concepts.title: Rotation – Turning About a Point
concepts.explanation:
A rotation turns a shape about a fixed point called the centre of rotation. Every point of the shape travels along a circular path around this centre, and every point turns through the same angle. A wheel spinning on its axle, a door swinging on its hinge, and the hands sweeping around a clock are all rotations. Like the other transformations, rotation keeps the shape congruent – the size and shape never change, only the orientation.

To describe a rotation fully you must give three pieces of information: the centre of rotation (the fixed point), the angle of rotation (how far to turn), and the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise). Miss any one of these and the description is incomplete. The most common angles are the quarter turn of 90°, the half turn of 180°, and the three-quarter turn of 270°. A half turn of 180° lands in the same place whether you go clockwise or anticlockwise, so for 180° the direction does not matter.

The distance from any point to the centre stays exactly the same through the whole turn. If a corner starts 5 units from the centre, it finishes 5 units from the centre, just pointing in a new direction. This is why tracing paper is the perfect tool for rotations: trace the shape, press your pencil tip firmly on the centre to hold it still, and turn the paper through the required angle. Where the tracing lands is the image.

For rotations about the origin, there are clean coordinate rules worth memorising. Here ‘anticlockwise’ is the positive direction, as usual in mathematics:

90° anticlockwise about the origin: (x, y) → (-y, x). So (3, 1) becomes (-1, 3).

180° about the origin (either direction): (x, y) → (-x, -y). So (3, 1) becomes (-3, -1).

90° clockwise about the origin, the same as 270° anticlockwise: (x, y) → (y, -x). So (3, 1) becomes (1, -3).
concepts.example: A shape has rotational symmetry when it looks identical after a turn of less than a full 360°. The order of rotational symmetry counts how many times it looks the same during one complete turn. A square has rotational symmetry of order 4, because it matches itself after 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. A regular pentagon has order 5, and an equilateral triangle has order 3. Look for this repeating balance in wheel hubs, flower petals, and the spokes of a fan.

concepts.title: Congruence and Combining Transformations
concepts.explanation:
The three transformations you have met – translation, reflection and rotation – are called rigid transformations because they never change a shape's size or its lengths and angles. The image is always congruent to the object. Two shapes are congruent when one can be placed exactly on top of the other after some combination of slides, flips and turns; every side matches a side, and every angle matches an angle. Congruence is one of the most important ideas in geometry, and transformations are the natural way to test for it.

Real problems often use more than one transformation in a row. When we do one transformation and then another, we call it a combination or composition of transformations. To carry one out, apply the first transformation to get an image, then apply the second transformation to that image. Work carefully and label each stage, for example A → A′ after the first move and A′ → A′′ after the second.

The order usually matters. Reflecting a shape and then translating it can land in a different place from translating first and then reflecting. Always read the instructions carefully to see which move comes first. There are, however, some neat results worth knowing. Two reflections in parallel mirror lines combine to give a single translation. Two reflections in mirror lines that cross combine to give a single rotation about the point where they meet. Mathematicians love these facts because they show how the transformations are secretly connected.

Every transformation also has an inverse – a move that undoes it and returns the shape home. The inverse of a translation is the same slide reversed. The inverse of a rotation is the same turn in the opposite direction about the same centre. The inverse of a reflection is simply the same reflection again, because flipping twice in the same mirror brings you back to the start. Understanding inverses helps you check your work: if you can undo a transformation and land exactly on the original, you did it correctly.

You have now met the whole toolkit of this unit: the coordinate grid with its four quadrants, accurate plotting and reading of points, and the three rigid transformations of translation, reflection and rotation, all held together by the idea of congruence. These ideas are not separate islands – they work as one system. A translation, a reflection and a rotation can all be written as a rule that acts on the coordinates (x, y), which is why a computer can perform millions of them every second when it draws a moving image on screen.

Think of how these pieces fit together in a single scene. A game designer places a spaceship using coordinates, slides it across the screen with a translation, flips it with a reflection when it turns to face the other way, and spins it with a rotation when it is hit. Every frame of the animation is just the same shape transformed by a new rule. When Maryam designs a repeating border pattern for a length of cloth, she reflects and translates one motif over and over, and the mathematics guarantees that every copy is perfectly congruent to the first.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these ideas into memory is to use them with real squared paper and real shapes. Plot a small triangle, then translate it, reflect it, and rotate it, checking each image with tracing paper. Say each move out loud with its full description – the vector for a slide, the mirror line for a flip, the centre, angle and direction for a turn. Every time you do this, your spatial reasoning grows stronger, and the geometry of later years will feel far more natural. Now let us practise together with some fully worked examples.

concepts.title: Finding the Distance Between Two Points
concepts.explanation: When two points share the same x-coordinate, they lie directly above or below each other on a vertical line, so the distance between them is just the difference between their y-coordinates. When two points share the same y-coordinate, they lie directly left or right of each other on a horizontal line, so the distance between them is the difference between their x-coordinates. Because distance is always positive, subtract the smaller value from the larger one (or take the absolute value of the difference) — you do not need to draw a grid to work this out.
concepts.example: Points A(3, 2) and B(3, 9) share the same x-coordinate, 3, so they lie on a vertical line. The distance between them is 9 − 2 = 7 units. Points C(−2, 5) and D(6, 5) share the same y-coordinate, 5, so they lie on a horizontal line. The distance between them is 6 − (−2) = 8 units.

concepts.title: Enlargement – Scaling a Shape Up
concepts.explanation: Enlargement is a transformation that changes the size of a shape without changing its angles or its overall proportions. Every length in the original shape (the object) is multiplied by the same number, called the scale factor, to give the matching length in the new shape (the image). This unit only uses positive whole-number scale factors, such as 2 or 3, which make the image bigger than the object. To enlarge a shape from a centre of enlargement, draw a line from the centre through each vertex of the object, and mark the image vertex at a distance from the centre that is the scale factor times as far as the object vertex was. Because every length is scaled by the same factor and every angle stays exactly the same, the image is similar to the object — same shape, same angles, but a different size. This is different from a translation, reflection or rotation, which all produce a congruent image (identical size).
concepts.example: Triangle ABC has vertices A(1, 1), B(2, 1) and C(1, 3). Enlarge it by scale factor 2 from the origin (0, 0). Multiply every coordinate by 2: A′(2, 2), B′(4, 2), C′(2, 6). Check the side lengths: AB was 1 unit long (from x = 1 to x = 2), and A′B′ is 2 units long (from x = 2 to x = 4) — exactly double, matching the scale factor. The image triangle A′B′C′ is similar to the original: it has the same angles, but every side is twice as long.

methods.title: How to plot a point
methods.example: In which quadrant does the point (-6, 4) lie?
steps: Start at the origin every time.
Move along the x-axis by the first number (right if positive, left if negative).
Move parallel to the y-axis by the second number (up if positive, down if negative).
Mark a small neat cross where you land.

methods.title: How to translate a shape
methods.example: A point P is 4 units left of the y-axis and 3 units below the x-axis. Write its coordinates.
steps: Read the vector: the top number is the horizontal move, the bottom is the vertical move.
Add the horizontal number to each x-coordinate.
Add the vertical number to each y-coordinate.
Plot the new vertices and join them in the same order.

methods.title: How to describe a rotation fully
methods.example: Triangle ABC has vertices A(2, 1), B(5, 1) and C(2, 4). Translate it by the vector (-3, 2). Give the image coordinates.
steps: State the centre of rotation (the fixed point).
State the angle of rotation (90°, 180° or 270°).
State the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise). For 180° the direction does not matter.

methods.title: Reflect in the y-axis
methods.example: Reflect the point Q(5, -2) in the y-axis.
steps: The rule for the y-axis is (x, y) → (-x, y).
Change the sign of x and keep y the same.
So Q(5, -2) becomes Q′(-5, -2).
Both points are 5 units from the y-axis, on opposite sides, at the same height.

methods.title: Reflect in a line x = 1
methods.example: Reflect the point R(4, 3) in the line x = 1.
steps: Find how far R is from the mirror line.
R has x = 4, and the line is x = 1, so R is 4 — 1 = 3 units to the right of the line.
The image must be 3 units to the left of the line: 1 — 3 = -2.
The y-coordinate is unchanged.

methods.title: Rotate 90° anticlockwise
methods.example: Rotate the point S(2, 1) by 90° anticlockwise about the origin.
steps: The rule for 90° anticlockwise about the origin is (x, y) → (-y, x).
So take S(2, 1): the new x is -y = -1, and the new y is x = 2.
Therefore S′ is (-1, 2).
Check with tracing paper: pin the origin and turn a quarter turn anticlockwise, and S lands at (-1, 2).

workedExamples.title: Name the quadrant
workedExamples.prompt: In which quadrant does the point (-6, 4) lie?
workedExamples.solution: The x-coordinate is negative (left of the y-axis) and the y-coordinate is positive (above the x-axis). Negative x with positive y is the top-left region, which is Quadrant II.

workedExamples.title: Plot and read
workedExamples.prompt: A point P is 4 units left of the y-axis and 3 units below the x-axis. Write its coordinates.
workedExamples.solution: Left of the y-axis means the x-coordinate is negative, so x = -4. Below the x-axis means the y-coordinate is negative, so y = -3. The point is P(-4, -3), which lies in Quadrant III.

workedExamples.title: Translate a triangle
workedExamples.prompt: Triangle ABC has vertices A(2, 1), B(5, 1) and C(2, 4). Translate it by the vector (-3, 2). Give the image coordinates.
workedExamples.solution: Add -3 to each x-coordinate and 2 to each y-coordinate. A(2, 1) → A′(-1, 3). B(5, 1) → B′(2, 3). C(2, 4) → C′(-1, 6). The image A′B′C′ is congruent to ABC and has simply slid 3 left and 2 up.

workedExamples.title: Reflect in the y-axis
workedExamples.prompt: Reflect the point Q(5, -2) in the y-axis.
workedExamples.solution: The rule for the y-axis is (x, y) → (-x, y). Change the sign of x and keep y the same. So Q(5, -2) becomes Q′(-5, -2). Both points are 5 units from the y-axis, on opposite sides, at the same height.

workedExamples.title: Reflect in a line x = 1
workedExamples.prompt: Reflect the point R(4, 3) in the line x = 1.
workedExamples.solution: Find how far R is from the mirror line. R has x = 4, and the line is x = 1, so R is 4 — 1 = 3 units to the right of the line. The image must be 3 units to the left of the line: 1 — 3 = -2. The y-coordinate is unchanged. So R′ is (-2, 3).

workedExamples.title: Rotate 90° anticlockwise
workedExamples.prompt: Rotate the point S(2, 1) by 90° anticlockwise about the origin.
workedExamples.solution: The rule for 90° anticlockwise about the origin is (x, y) → (-y, x). So take S(2, 1): the new x is -y = -1, and the new y is x = 2. Therefore S′ is (-1, 2). Check with tracing paper: pin the origin and turn a quarter turn anticlockwise, and S lands at (-1, 2).

workedExamples.title: Rotate 180°
workedExamples.prompt: Rotate the point T(-3, 5) by 180° about the origin.
workedExamples.solution: The rule for 180° about the origin is (x, y) → (-x, -y). Change both signs. So T(-3, 5) becomes T′(3, -5). A half turn sends every point straight through the origin to the opposite side, the same distance away.

workedExamples.title: Combine two transformations
workedExamples.prompt: Point U(1, 2) is first reflected in the x-axis, then translated by (4, 1). Find the final image.
workedExamples.solution: Do the reflection first. Reflecting in the x-axis uses (x, y) → (x, -y), so U(1, 2) → U′(1, -2). Now translate U′ by (4, 1): add 4 to the x and 1 to the y, giving U′′(5, -1). The final image is U′′(5, -1). Notice the order mattered — doing the translation first would have given a different point.

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: Rotate the point (1, 0) by 90° anticlockwise about the origin.
workedExamples.solution: The rule for 90° anticlockwise about the origin is (x, y) → (-y, x). So take (1, 0): the new x is -y = 0, and the new y is x = 1. Therefore the image is A′(0, 1).

workedExamples.title: Reflect the point (6, 2) in the line x = 3
workedExamples.prompt: Reflect the point (6, 2) in the line x = 3.
workedExamples.solution: Find how far (6, 2) is from the mirror line x = 3. The point has x = 6, so it is 6 — 3 = 3 units to the right of the line. The image must be 3 units to the left of the line: 3 — 3 = 0. The y-coordinate is unchanged. So the image is B′(0, 2).

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: Describe fully the single transformation that maps (2, 3) onto (2, -3).
workedExamples.solution: The x-coordinate stays the same (2) and the y-coordinate changes sign (3 becomes -3). The rule (x, y) → (x, -y) is reflection in the x-axis. So the single transformation is: reflection in the x-axis.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Point P(4, -2) is rotated 90° clockwise about the origin, then translated by (1, 5). Find the final coordinates.
workedExamples.solution: 1) 90° clockwise uses (x, y) → (y, -x), so (4, -2) → (-2, -4). Then translate by (1, 5): add 1 to the x-coordinate and 5 to the y-coordinate: (-2 + 1, -4 + 5) = (-1, 1). The final coordinates are (-1, 1).

activities.title: Draw Your Own Four-Quadrant Grid
activities.materials: squared paper, a ruler, a pencil.
steps: Draw an x-axis and a y-axis crossing at the centre of the page. Label the origin (0, 0).
Number both axes from -6 to 6, marking each unit carefully.
Plot one point in each quadrant and label its coordinates.
Challenge a family member (or your AI tutor) to name the quadrant of each point you plotted.
Keep your grid – you can reuse it for the transformation activities below.

activities.title: Coordinate Picture Reveal
steps: Secretly choose a simple picture, such as a house or a boat, made from straight lines.
Write down the list of coordinates for each corner, in order.
Give only the list of coordinates to a friend or your AI tutor and ask them to plot and join the points.
Check whether the picture they reveal matches your secret drawing.
This game trains fast, accurate plotting and reading of points in all four quadrants.

activities.title: Tracing-Paper Transformations
activities.materials: squared paper, tracing paper (or thin baking paper), a pencil.
steps: Draw a small triangle on your grid and label its vertices.
Trace the triangle, then slide the tracing to test a translation – read off the new coordinates.
Pin the tracing at the origin with your pencil tip and turn it 90° and 180° to test rotations.
Tracing paper is the tool professionals wish they had in exams – use it to check every transformation you draw.

activities.title: Transformation Treasure Hunt (Family Game)
activities.materials: a room, some small objects, and slips of paper.
steps: Mark a starting spot as the origin and agree which way is positive x and positive y.
Write instructions as vectors, such as ‘translate by (3, -2) steps’, leading to a hidden treasure.
Let a family member (or, if nobody is free, your AI tutor) follow the clues to find the treasure, then swap roles.

activities.title: Symmetry Hunt and Pattern Design
activities.materials: your eyes, a notebook, and later some coloured pencils.
steps: Walk around your home and find five objects with line symmetry or rotational symmetry – tiles, mats, windows, cups.
For each one, sketch it and mark the lines of symmetry or state the order of rotational symmetry.
Now design your own repeating border pattern by reflecting and translating one small motif.
Colour your pattern and explain which transformations you used to make it.

activities.title: Investigation – Combining Two Reflections
activities.materials: squared paper, tracing paper, a ruler.
steps: Draw two parallel vertical mirror lines a few units apart, and a small shape to the left of both.
Reflect the shape in the first line, then reflect the image in the second line.
Measure how far the final image has moved from the original – what single transformation is this?
Now try two mirror lines that cross at a point, and describe the single transformation you get instead.
Write down what you discover – you have found two of the most elegant results in transformation geometry.

rules.title: Avoiding Coordinate Mix-Ups
rules.text: Here is a common trap to avoid. Many learners rush and swap the two numbers, plotting (2, 5) where (5, 2) belongs. Slow down and whisper the rule – x first, then y; along, then up. Another trap is to lose track of the sign when working in the lower or left quadrants. If Khadija plots the vertices of a triangle and one corner drifts into the wrong quadrant, the whole triangle will look wrong. Careful, unhurried plotting is the foundation of every transformation that follows in this unit.

rules.title: The Mirror Line Rule
rules.text: The mirror line follows one golden rule: every point of the image is the same distance from the mirror line as the matching point of the object, but on the opposite side. The line joining a point to its image crosses the mirror line at a right angle. So if a corner sits 3 units to the left of the mirror line, its image sits 3 units to the right of that same line, directly across from it.

rules.title: Reflecting in the x-axis
rules.text: Reflection in the x-axis: the rule is (x, y) → (x, -y). The x stays the same; the y changes sign. So (3, 2) becomes (3, -2).

rules.title: Reflecting in the y-axis
rules.text: Reflection in the y-axis: the rule is (x, y) → (-x, y). The y stays the same; the x changes sign. So (3, 2) becomes (-3, 2).

rules.title: Summary of the Unit Toolkit
rules.text: You have now met the whole toolkit of this unit: the coordinate grid with its four quadrants, accurate plotting and reading of points, and the three rigid transformations of translation, reflection and rotation, all held together by the idea of congruence. These ideas are not separate islands – they work as one system. A translation, a reflection and a rotation can all be written as a rule that acts on the coordinates (x, y), which is why a computer can perform millions of them every second when it draws a moving image on screen.

rules.title: Transformations in Action
rules.text: Think of how these pieces fit together in a single scene. A game designer places a spaceship using coordinates, slides it across the screen with a translation, flips it with a reflection when it turns to face the other way, and spins it with a rotation when it is hit. Every frame of the animation is just the same shape transformed by a new rule. When Maryam designs a repeating border pattern for a length of cloth, she reflects and translates one motif over and over, and the mathematics guarantees that every copy is perfectly congruent to the first.

realProblems.answer: Ibrahim's image: 90° anticlockwise uses (x, y) → (-y, x), so (3, 1) → (-1, 3). Zahra's image: 90° clockwise uses (x, y) → (y, -x), so (3, 1) → (1, -3). realProblems.prompt: A shape is reflected in the x-axis and its image is then reflected in the x-axis again. Explain, using the idea of inverse transformations, why the shape returns exactly to its starting position.

Reflection is a self-inverse transformation, so two reflections in the same mirror line cancel out and the shape returns exactly to its starting position.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 1) 90° clockwise uses (x, y) → (y, -x), so (4, -2) → (-2, -4). Then translate by (1, 5): (-2 + 1, -4 + 5) = (-1, 1). The final coordinates are (-1, 1).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A shape is translated by (-3, 4) and then by (7, -1). Write the single equivalent vector and the vector that returns it to the start.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The single equivalent vector is (-3 + 7, 4 + (-1)) = (4, 3). The vector that returns the shape to the start is the inverse of this, (-4, -3).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: The point (a, b) is rotated 180° about the origin to give (-6, 9). Find a and b.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 180° rotation maps (a, b) to (-a, -b). Since (-a, -b) = (-6, 9), we get a = 6 and b = -9. So the original point is (6, -9).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Two reflections in parallel vertical mirror lines are performed one after the other. Explain what single transformation this is equivalent to.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Two reflections in parallel vertical mirror lines are equivalent to a single translation. The translation is horizontal (perpendicular to the mirror lines), and its distance is twice the distance between the two mirror lines.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Rotation – Turning About a Point.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A rotation turns a shape about a fixed point called the centre of rotation. Every point of the shape travels along a circular path around this centre, and every point turns through the same angle. A wheel spinning on its axle, a door swinging on its hinge, and the hands sweeping around a clock are all rotations. Like the other transformations, rotation keeps the shape congruent – the size and shape never change, only the orientation. To describe a rotation fully you must give three pieces of information: the centre of rotation, the angle turned through, and the direction of the turn (clockwise or anticlockwise).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Congruence and Combining Transformations.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The three transformations you have met – translation, reflection and rotation – are called rigid transformations because they never change a shape's size or its lengths and angles. The image is always congruent to the object. Two shapes are congruent when one can be placed exactly on top of the other after some combination of slides, flips and turns; every side matches a side, and every angle matches an angle. Congruence is one of the most important ideas in geometry, and transformations are the natural way to show that two shapes are congruent, since a rigid transformation is exactly the sequence of moves that carries one shape exactly onto the other.

games.title: Challenge Cards: Rotation
games.description: Practise rotation through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which single rule maps (x, y) to (x, -y)?
choices: Reflection in the x-axis
Reflection in the y-axis
Rotation 180° about the origin
Translation by (0, -1)
rounds.answer: Reflection in the x-axis
rounds.clue: Ask yourself what "Coordinates" means here before you choose.
rounds.explanation: (x, y) → (x, -y) keeps x the same and changes the sign of y, which is reflection in the x-axis.

rounds.prompt: Point B lies in Quadrant IV. What must be true about its x- and y-coordinates?
choices: x is positive and y is negative
x is negative and y is positive
Both x and y are positive
Both x and y are negative
rounds.answer: x is positive and y is negative
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: Quadrant IV is to the right of the y-axis (positive x) and below the x-axis (negative y).

games.title: Think Fast: Vector

rounds.prompt: A shape is translated and then rotated. What can you say about the image compared with the original shape?
choices: It is congruent to the original
It is larger than the original
It is smaller than the original
Its side lengths change but its angles stay the same
rounds.answer: It is congruent to the original
rounds.clue: Ask yourself what "Coordinates" means here before you choose.
rounds.explanation: Translations and rotations are rigid transformations, so the image is always congruent to the object – the same size and shape.

selfAssessment: I can plot and read points in all four quadrants using coordinate pairs (x, y), including negative values.
I can name the origin, the x-axis, the y-axis and the four quadrants, and know the sign pattern of each quadrant.
I can describe and perform a translation using a column vector and describe it in words.
I can describe and perform a reflection in a mirror line, including the x-axis, the y-axis and lines such as x = 2.
I can describe and perform a rotation about a point, giving the centre, angle and direction.
I can use coordinate rules to transform points quickly with algebra.
I can explain why translations, reflections and rotations produce a congruent image, and combine two transformations in sequence.
